theory.intro: A sample is **biased** when it does not fairly represent the population. This can give a misleading result. Bias can come from who ends up in the sample or from how questions are worded.
facts: **Selection bias** — where, when or how the group was chosen makes it misrepresent the population (surveying only the basketball team about height).
**Volunteer bias** — people decide whether to take part, so those with a strong opinion or special interest may be more likely to reply (a click-to-vote online poll).
**Survivorship bias** — only the cases that lasted or succeeded are in the data (judging a gym by its members, after the unhappy ones quit).
**Small sample size** — too few people are asked to show the variety in the population (asking $3$ shoppers what a whole suburb wants). A small sample may miss important views.
**Leading question** — praise, emotional language or one-sided information pushes towards an answer ('Do you agree that this brilliant plan should go ahead?').
**Ambiguous question** — the wording can be read two ways, because a time period or boundary is missing ('How often do you exercise?').
**Not enough choices** — the response options leave out answers people would give, such as a neutral or negative option.
Options that overlap are also a fault, because one value then fits two boxes.
A **larger sample does not remove bias** — the same unfair selection is simply repeated more times.
To diagnose bias, name which group is left out or over-represented, or which words push an answer. Explain how this may affect the result.

workedExamples.question_text:
Name the main bias in each method and explain.
(a) To find all students’ favourite sport, a school asks only its basketball team.
(b) A council puts a vote on its website and waits for residents to choose to reply.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) **Selection bias**: basketball players are over-represented and may favour basketball more than students in general.
(b) **Volunteer bias**: residents choose whether to reply. Those with strong opinions may be more likely to take part.

workedExamples.question_text:
Name the main problem with each sample.
(a) A factory studies how long its machines last by inspecting only machines still working after ten years. Machines that failed earlier were scrapped.
(b) To find the views of $420$ residents, a council asks only $2$ of them.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) **Survivorship bias**: the machines that failed early are missing, so only the survivors are studied.
(b) **Small sample size**: two residents may not show the range of views in the town.

workedExamples.question_text:
Identify the fault and rewrite each question fairly.
(a) "Do you agree that our brilliant new library should stay open?"
(b) "How often do you visit the library?"
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) **Leading question**: "brilliant" praises the library and pushes towards agreement. A fair version is "Should the new library stay open?"
(b) **Ambiguous question**: no time period is given. A clearer version is "How many times did you visit the library in the past week?"

workedExamples.question_text:
Explain the problem in each survey and suggest an improvement.
(a) A service rating offers only Good, Very good and Excellent.
(b) Spending groups are $0$–$10$, $10$–$20$ and $20$–$30$, with both ends included.
(c) A club says $4000$ voluntary online replies cannot be biased.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) **Not enough choices**: unhappy customers have no suitable answer. Include negative and neutral ratings as well as positive ones.
(b) **Overlapping choices**: $10$ and $20$ each fit two groups. State boundaries so each amount fits only one group, and allow amounts outside the listed range.
(c) A large number does not remove **volunteer bias**. Choose members at random from the full membership list and contact them directly instead of relying only on voluntary online replies.

foundation.question_text:
A reporter wants to know what proportion of Australian adults have a full-time job.
She surveys shoppers at a shopping centre at $11$ am on a Tuesday.
Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Many adults with full-time jobs will be at work at $11$ am on a Tuesday, so surveying only shoppers at that time may under-represent them.
**Selection bias.**

foundation.question_text:
A news website asks readers to click a link to vote on whether a new stadium should be built.
Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Readers choose whether to click the link. Those with strong opinions may be more likely to reply.
**Volunteer bias.**

foundation.question_text:
A council asks $3$ shoppers at a shopping centre whether a new car park is needed, then reports that residents want one.
Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Three shoppers may not show the range of opinions held across a whole suburb.
**Small sample size.**

foundation.question_text:
A gym wants to measure satisfaction among everyone who has held a membership this year. It surveys only current members, leaving out people who cancelled because they were unhappy.
Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
The unhappy members who cancelled are left out, so the survey includes only the members who stayed.
**Survivorship bias.**

foundation.question_text:
A council asks the members of the local cycling club whether more cycle lanes should be built.
Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Cycling club members are far more likely to want cycle lanes than residents in general.
**Selection bias.**

foundation.question_text: A product-review form asks: 'How much did you enjoy our brilliant new blender?' Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
The words 'brilliant' and 'enjoy' assume the customer liked the blender and push towards a positive answer.
**Leading question.**

foundation.question_text: A product-review form asks: 'How often do you use your blender?' Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
No time period is given, so 'often' could mean per day, per week or per month, and different customers answer different questions.
**Ambiguous question.**

foundation.question_text:
A product-review form asks customers to rate a blender, offering only the options **Good**, **Very good** and **Excellent**.
Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
A customer who disliked the blender has no option that fits, so every response recorded looks positive.
**Not enough choices.**

development.question_text:
A video channel with $200\,000$ followers asks its followers whether its videos have improved this year.
Explain why the sample is unrepresentative.
development.solution_text:
Followers already like the channel enough to follow it. People who stopped watching or do not follow it are not asked.
**The sample over-represents fans, so the responses may be more positive than those of viewers in general.**

development.question_text:
A survey about how Australian workers travel to work interviews only workers who arrived by car at a shopping centre.
State one group likely to be under-represented, and say whether the proportion who drive to work is likely to be over-estimated or under-estimated.
development.solution_text:
Workers who use trains, ride or walk may be under-represented because only people who arrived by car are asked.
**The proportion who drive to work is likely to be over-estimated.**

development.question_text:
A running club emails a training survey only to the members who finished last year's marathon, asking whether the training program works.
Name the bias, and describe one change that would fix it.
development.solution_text:
The members who withdrew or did not finish are missing, so only the successes are counted.
**Survivorship bias.**
The club should also survey the members who withdrew or did not finish, so the failures are included.

development.question_text: An online poll asks: 'Given that plastic bags are choking our oceans, should the shop charge for them?' Name the fault in the question, and rewrite it fairly.
development.solution_text:
The question supplies one-sided emotional information before asking, pushing the reader towards 'yes'.
**Leading question.**
A fair version is 'Should the shop charge for plastic bags?'

development.question_text:
A product-review form asks how much a customer spent, offering the boxes \$0–\$10, \$10–\$20 and \$20–\$30.
Explain why the responses will be unreliable.
development.solution_text:
The boxes overlap, so a customer who spent \$10 can tick either of the first two.
**The question is ambiguous, and two customers who spent the same amount can end up counted in different groups.**

development.question_text:
A fitness app shows a pop-up asking users to rate it, and only the users who choose to reply do so.
The app's users are all people who already exercise regularly.
Name the bias that comes from **who chose to reply**, and explain it.
development.solution_text:
Users decide for themselves whether to answer the pop-up. Those with strong opinions may be more likely to reply.
**Volunteer bias.**
That every user already exercises regularly is a separate selection problem, not the bias asked for here.

development.question_text:
A phone company wants to measure satisfaction among everyone who has been a customer this year. It surveys only current customers, leaving out customers who left because they were unhappy.
Name the type of bias, and state the likely effect on the satisfaction rating.
development.solution_text:
The unhappy customers who left are missing from the survey.
**Survivorship bias. The satisfaction rating is likely to be higher than a rating that also includes those customers.**

mastery.question_text:
A skateboard company reports that $96\%$ of the reviews on its website give its new deck $4$ stars or more.
Only customers who registered the deck may leave a review, and the company deletes the reviews of customers who returned the deck for a refund.
Name the bias created by **deleting the returned-deck reviews**, and explain why the $96\%$ cannot be used to claim that most buyers are happy.
mastery.solution_text:
The returned-deck reviews are deleted, so only reviews of decks that were kept remain.
This is **survivorship bias**. Buyers who returned the deck may be less satisfied, but their reviews cannot be counted.
The $96\%$ describes only the reviews that remain. It cannot show satisfaction among all buyers.

mastery.question_text:
An online poll asks: 'Given that the new stadium will cost \$800 million, do you agree that the money is wasted?' The only responses offered are **Agree** and **Strongly agree**.
Identify two separate faults in this poll and explain the effect of each.
mastery.solution_text:
The one-sided cost information and the words "money is wasted" push the reader towards agreeing.
**Leading question.**
Both options agree. A reader who disagrees has no suitable response.
**Not enough choices.**
Every recorded response must agree, while readers who disagree may not respond at all.

mastery.question_text:
A club committee says its online poll cannot be biased because $5000$ members responded.
Explain why a large number of responses does not rule out bias, and describe a method that would reduce this problem.
mastery.solution_text:
The members chose whether to answer. Members with strong opinions may be more likely to reply, even when there are $5000$ responses.
**A large number of responses does not remove volunteer bias.**
Choose members at random from the full membership list and contact them directly, rather than relying only on members who click the poll.
